contentSections: Quick answer

A corner plot house has two faces on the street, so its elevation must work from two directions at once. The best corner plot house elevation design treats the corner as the main feature, wraps the same material language around both sides, and uses louvers, fins or balconies to manage privacy and sun. Treat the two street faces as one composition, not as a front and a side.
Key takeaways

• The corner is the hero. People see it first, from far away, so design it with care. • Keep one clear material idea across both faces, with one or two accents. • Corner plots often get more sun and more street noise, so shading and privacy matter. • Check local bylaws for setbacks, projections and corner rules before you finalise the design.
Why corner plots are different

On a normal plot, you design one front and treat the sides plainly. On a corner plot, the second street face is just as visible, and the point where the two meet is seen from both roads. Poor design shows up immediately: a plain side wall next to a rich front, or a flat corner with nothing to hold the eye.
Corner plots also have practical advantages: more light, more cross ventilation and more openings. A good elevation uses these without exposing the family to the street.
Idea 1: Make the corner a feature
Let the corner carry the main design move. Options include:

• A vertical corner element in a contrasting material, running from ground to roof. • A cut or chamfered corner that softens the turn and opens up the view. • A corner balcony or projecting volume, which also creates shade below. For how projecting forms are built, see our guide to cantilever facade design.
Idea 2: Wrap one material across both faces

Use one main cladding across both street faces so the house reads as one building. Add a second material only as an accent at the entrance or the corner. Our article on front elevation design ideas explains material zoning, which works well here.
Idea 3: Use fins and louvers for privacy and sun

Corner plots often face two orientations, so shading is useful. Vertical fins can screen windows that face a busy road while still letting light in. Horizontal louvers cut high sun. Both give the elevation depth through shadow. See architectural fins design for how fins shape a facade, and balcony louver design ideas for balcony screens.
Idea 4: Balance solid and open areas

Too much glass on a corner can feel exposed. Too much solid wall feels heavy. Mix solid cladding, perforated or slatted screens and glazing, so the house feels open to light but private from the street.
Idea 5: Plan the entrance and gate together
On a corner plot, choose which street carries the main entrance and design the gate, boundary wall and facade as one. A second, quieter entry on the other street can serve cars or service access.
Idea 6: Light the corner at night

A corner is visible from two roads at night too. Warm graze lighting along the cladding, a lit entrance and a softly lit corner feature make the house easy to find and add safety. Plan cables and fixings at design stage so finished cladding is not drilled later.

Corner detailing that makes the difference

The turn is where cladding is hardest to do well. Panels should meet at the corner with a planned joint, either a clean shadow gap or a folded return, and the sub-frame behind must be accurate there. A wrap-around corner also takes higher local wind pressure, so fixings may need extra attention in taller houses. Ask your facade company to show the corner detail on a drawing before production.

A corner plot has two faces to clad, so the area, and the cost, is usually higher than a single-front house. Read our metal facade cost guide for what drives the price. Mistakes to avoid

• Designing a rich front and a blank side wall • A flat corner with no focal point • Large glass on a busy road side, with no screening • Too many materials competing at the turn • Ignoring local rules on setbacks and projections
Frequently asked questions

1. What is the best elevation for a corner plot house?

One that treats the corner as the main feature and wraps a consistent material across both street faces, with shading and privacy screens where needed.

2. How do I design a G plus 1 corner house elevation?

Keep the ground floor solid and welcoming at the entrance, and use the upper floor for a balcony, fins or louvers at the corner. Match the material on both faces.

3. Which materials are good for a corner plot elevation?

Coated aluminium, perforated or slatted metal and fluted panels all work well, with stone or textured plaster as a base.

4. Do I need approval for a corner balcony or projection?

Rules vary by city and plot. Check local bylaws and your architect’s advice before finalising projections.

5. Does a corner plot cost more to clad?

Usually, because it has two street faces and more area. Ask for a quotation based on your drawings.
